A superkey may carry extra attributes, so it need not be a candidate key; a relation can have several candidate keys; and adding an attribute to a candidate key gives a superkey that is no longer minimal.

questions.stem: Takes(sid, cid) holds (s1, c1), (s1, c2), (s1, c4), (s2, c1), (s2, c2), (s2, c3), (s3, c1), (s3, c2), (s3, c3), (s3, c4) and (s4, c4). Course(cid, dept) holds (c1, CS), (c2, CS), (c3, EE) and (c4, CS). How many tuples are in $\text{Takes} \div \pi_{cid}(\sigma_{dept=\text{'CS'}}(\text{Course}))$?
questions.explanation: The divisor is the set of CS courses {c1, c2, c4}. s1 takes c1, c2 and c4, so it qualifies. s2 lacks c4, and s4 takes only c4. s3 takes all three; its extra course c3 does not matter. The result is {s1, s3}: 2 tuples.

questions.stem: Enrolled(sid, cid) records which student takes which course, and Course(cid, title) lists all courses. What does $\text{Enrolled} \div \pi_{cid}(\text{Course})$ return?
options: The students enrolled in at least one course
The courses in which every student is enrolled
The students enrolled in every course
The students enrolled in no course
questions.explanation: Division keeps the attribute that is not in the divisor, sid, and returns the sid values that Enrolled pairs with every cid of the divisor. That is the 'for all' query: the students who take every course.

questions.stem: R(A, B) holds (1, a), (2, b), (3, a) and (4, c). S(B, C) holds (a, x), (a, y), (b, z) and (d, w). How many tuples are in the full outer natural join R ⟗ S?
questions.explanation: The inner natural join on B gives (1, a, x), (1, a, y), (3, a, x), (3, a, y) and (2, b, z): 5 tuples. R's tuple (4, c) has no partner and is kept as (4, c, NULL); S's tuple (d, w) is kept as (NULL, d, w). Total 5 + 1 + 1 = 7.

questions.stem: R(A, B) has 50 tuples and S(B, C) has 20 tuples. B is the primary key of S, and R.B is a NOT NULL foreign key referencing S. How many tuples does the natural join R ⋈ S contain?
options: Exactly 20
Exactly 50
Exactly 1000
Anywhere from 0 to 1000
questions.explanation: Because B is a key of S, each R tuple matches at most one S tuple; because R.B is a NOT NULL foreign key, it matches at least one. So every R tuple appears exactly once: 50 tuples. Without the key and foreign-key facts the bound would only be 0 to 50 × 20 = 1000.

questions.stem: R and S are union-compatible relations with attributes (A, B), and p is a condition on A only. Which equalities hold for every instance of R and S?
options: $\pi_A(R \cup S) = \pi_A(R) \cup \pi_A(S)$
$\pi_A(R - S) = \pi_A(R) - \pi_A(S)$
$\sigma_p(R - S) = \sigma_p(R) - S$
$\pi_A(R \cap S) = \pi_A(R) \cap \pi_A(S)$
questions.explanation: An A-value comes from R ∪ S exactly when it comes from R or from S, so projection distributes over union. A tuple is in σp(R − S) when it is in R, not in S and satisfies p, which is exactly membership in σp(R) − S. Projection does not distribute over difference or intersection: with R = {(1, x)} and S = {(1, y)}, πA(R − S) = {1} but πA(R) − πA(S) = ∅, and πA(R ∩ S) = ∅ but πA(R) ∩ πA(S) = {1}.

questions.stem: R(A, B) and S(A, B) are relations. Which tuple relational calculus expression is unsafe?
options: {t | t ∈ R ∨ t ∈ S}
questions.explanation: {t | ¬(t ∈ R)} asks for every possible tuple that is not in R: infinitely many tuples, built from values that appear nowhere in the database. The other three take every result tuple from R or S; they are a selection, a difference and a union.

questions.stem: Emp(eid, name, age). Which TRC expression returns the same relation as $\pi_{name}(\sigma_{age > 30}(\text{Emp}))$?
options: {t | t ∈ Emp ∧ t.age > 30}
{t | ∃e ∈ Emp (e.age > 30 ∧ t.name = e.name)}
{t | ∀e ∈ Emp (e.age > 30 ∧ t.name = e.name)}
{t | ∃e ∈ Emp (e.age > 30) ∧ ∃f ∈ Emp (t.name = f.name)}
questions.explanation: The projection keeps only name, so t must have that single attribute, copied from an Emp tuple that passes the selection: ∃e ∈ Emp (e.age > 30 ∧ t.name = e.name). {t | t ∈ Emp ∧ t.age > 30} returns whole Emp tuples with all three attributes. The ∀ version demands that every employee be over 30 and share t's name. The last option tests the two conditions on different tuples, so once anyone is over 30 it returns every employee's name.

questions.stem: Emp(eid, did) holds (1, 10), (2, 20) and (3, NULL). Dept(did, dname) holds (10, CS) and (30, EE). Which describes the natural left outer join Emp ⟕ Dept?
options: 1 tuple: (1, 10, CS)
3 tuples, only 1 of which has dname = NULL
4 tuples: the 3 Emp tuples plus (NULL, 30, EE)
3 tuples, 2 of which have dname = NULL
questions.explanation: A left outer join keeps every Emp tuple. (1, 10) matches and gives (1, 10, CS). (2, 20) finds no department 20, and (3, NULL) cannot match anything because NULL equals nothing, so both are padded: (2, 20, NULL) and (3, NULL, NULL). Dept's unmatched (30, EE) appears only in a right or full outer join.

questions.stem: Emp(eid, salary) has key eid. What does $\pi_{eid}(\text{Emp}) - \pi_{E1.eid}(\sigma_{E1.salary < E2.salary}(\rho_{E1}(\text{Emp}) \times \rho_{E2}(\text{Emp})))$ return?
options: The employees with the highest salary, including all who tie for it
The employees with the lowest salary
Every employee except those with the highest salary
The employees whose salary differs from every other employee's
questions.explanation: The product pairs every employee E1 with every employee E2, and the selection keeps the pairs where E1 earns less than E2. Projecting E1.eid lists everyone who earns less than somebody. Subtracting them from all employees leaves those whom nobody out-earns: the maximum-salary employees, ties included. With > in place of < the expression would return the minimum instead.

questions.stem: Student(sid, name), Course(cid) and Enrolled(sid, cid) are relations, and Course is non-empty. Which relational algebra expression returns the same result as {t | t ∈ Student ∧ ∀c ∈ Course ∃e ∈ Enrolled (e.sid = t.sid ∧ e.cid = c.cid)}?
options: $\text{Student} \bowtie (\text{Enrolled} \div \text{Course})$
$\text{Student} \bowtie \pi_{sid}(\text{Enrolled})$
$\text{Student} \bowtie (\pi_{sid}(\text{Enrolled}) - (\text{Enrolled} \div \text{Course}))$
$\pi_{sid,name}(\text{Student} \times \text{Course})$
questions.explanation: The calculus query keeps a student when every course has a matching Enrolled tuple: a 'for all' query, hence division. Enrolled ÷ Course returns the sid values paired with every cid, and the natural join with Student adds the name. Joining with πsid(Enrolled) means 'at least one course', and the third option is 'some but not all'. The non-empty condition matters: with no courses the calculus query returns every student, but the division returns only students with some enrollment.

questions.stem: Emp(eid, dept, sal) holds the tuples (1, 1, 50), (2, 1, 70), (3, 2, 60), (4, 2, 40), (5, 3, 80) and (6, 3, 60). How many tuples does {t | t ∈ Emp ∧ ∀s ∈ Emp (s.dept = 2 ⇒ t.sal > s.sal)} return?
questions.explanation: The implication constrains t only against the dept-2 employees, whose salaries are 60 and 40, so t qualifies when t.sal > 60. That holds for eid 2 (70) and eid 5 (80). Eid 3 and eid 6 earn exactly 60 and fail the strict >; with ≥ the count would be 4. Reading ⇒ as ∧ demands that every employee be in dept 2 and returns 0 tuples.

questions.stem: R(A, B) and S(A, B) are relations, and an unrestricted tuple variable ranges over every tuple of the domain, which always contains tuples outside S. Which expressions are equivalent to {t | t ∈ R ∧ ∀s ∈ S (s.B > t.B)} on every instance?
options: {t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬∃s ∈ S (s.B ≤ t.B)}
{t | t ∈ R ∧ ∀s (s ∈ S ⇒ s.B > t.B)}
{t | t ∈ R ∧ ∀s (s ∈ S ∧ s.B > t.B)}
{t | t ∈ R ∧ ∃s (s ∈ S ⇒ s.B > t.B)}
questions.explanation: ∀s ∈ S (P) ≡ ¬∃s ∈ S (¬P), and the negation of s.B > t.B is s.B ≤ t.B, so the first form matches. The bounded ∀ unrolls to ∀s (s ∈ S ⇒ P), so the second matches. The third demands that every tuple of the domain be in S, which fails, so it always returns ∅. In the fourth, any tuple outside S makes the implication true, so it returns all of R.

pitfalls.text: Natural join matches on every attribute with the same name. If the relations share no attribute it silently becomes a Cartesian product; if they share an unintended one, matches disappear.
Division has 'all of' semantics and returns only the attributes that are not in the divisor. An empty divisor makes every candidate qualify.
Outer joins pad unmatched tuples with NULLs, and a NULL join value matches nothing, not even another NULL. A later selection on a padded attribute throws those tuples away again.
A superkey need not be minimal: every candidate key is a superkey, but a superkey with a removable attribute is not a candidate key.
Relational algebra projection removes duplicates because relations are sets, so a projection can return fewer tuples than its input. SQL's SELECT keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is written.
When counting tables, a 1:N relationship becomes a foreign key on the N side and needs no table, while every M:N relationship and every multivalued attribute needs its own.
Unrestricted quantifiers pair ∃ with ∧ and ∀ with ⇒. Writing ∀s (s ∈ R ∧ P) makes the query empty, and ∃s (s ∈ R ⇒ P) makes the condition always true.

revisionCard.heading: ER to relations
lines: Entity set, strong or weak → one relation; weak key = owner key + discriminator
1:N → foreign key on the N side; 1:1 → foreign key on either side, or one merged relation when at least one side is total
M:N → own relation keyed on both entity keys; multivalued attribute → own relation
Derived attributes are not stored; double line = total participation

revisionCard.heading: Keys
lines: Candidate key = minimal superkey; primary key = the chosen candidate key (unique, NOT NULL)
One candidate key of k attributes among n → 2^(n − k) superkeys
Foreign key value = an existing referenced key value, or NULL

revisionCard.heading: Relational algebra
lines: Basic: σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ; R ∩ S = R − (R − S)
θ-join = σθ(R × S); natural join equates all common attributes
Outer joins pad with NULL; R ÷ S answers 'for all' queries

revisionCard.heading: Tuple calculus
lines: {t | P(t)} with ∃ and ∀; only t is free
Safe: every result value comes from the database or the query's constants
Maximum: t ∈ R ∧ ¬∃s ∈ R (s.A > t.A), ties kept

errata.claim: Division is the inverse of Cartesian product and returns the tuples in the left relation that pair with every tuple in the right.
errata.correction: R ÷ S does not return tuples of R. Its schema is X = attrs(R) − attrs(S), and it returns each x such that (x, y) ∈ R for every y ∈ S. It inverts a product only in the sense that (R × S) ÷ S = R for non-empty S; in general (R ÷ S) × S ⊆ R.

errata.claim: A safe TRC expression is one in which all tuples of the result come from the database.
errata.correction: Safety concerns values, not stored tuples: every value in the result must belong to dom(P), the constants of the formula plus the values in the relations it mentions. Result tuples need not be stored tuples; {t | ∃s ∈ R (t.A = s.A)} builds new one-attribute tuples and is safe, while {t | ¬(t ∈ R)} is unsafe.
